headline: New moon springs building — bass window reopens as bonito push into Narragansett Bay
subhead: The cold wall between the Island and the Sound finally broke, and that's changing everything from the North Rip to Beavertail.
body_markdown:
Last week the wind did what it usually does in early July — it went southwest and sat there, five, six days of it, pushing warm surface water up against the Island and stirring the upper water column just enough to keep the stripers honest but not stupid. Tides were still on the tail end of the last cycle, moderate swings, nothing dramatic. But the real story wasn't the wind — it was what happened to the cold wall that usually sits between Block Island Sound and Rhode Island Sound this time of year. That thermal barrier collapsed, better than ten degrees in the RIS side, and when that wall goes down, everything south of Newport gets an invitation it doesn't usually get until August. Bonito and Spanish mackerel don't read charts, they read water, and right now the water between here and Point Judith says come on in.

This week the moon is going dark, working toward new phase around the 11th, and that means the tides are building toward springs — bigger swings, stronger current, and a sunset flood that's going to stack up perfectly with high water on the western approaches by Friday through Monday. That's the window I'm circling. Big fish don't move on comfort, they move on current speed and light angle, and a new-moon spring flood hitting right at dusk is about as good a combination as this Island produces. Water temps have been stable to slightly warming inshore, mid-60s holding around the ledges, upwelled water running closer to 60 out on the North Rip edge where the bottom drops fast — that seam is exactly why the biggest bass in the Northeast show up here every July and nowhere else.

Striper fishing has been solid, not explosive, but solid — which at this point in July is exactly what I expect. The North Rip is still holding fish on the drop of the tide, working eels and 3-ounce bucktails with white curly tails down through 25 to 40 feet where the rip stacks bait against the ledge. Southwest Ledge has been better on the last two hours of the incoming, live scup and pogies drifted naturally through the structure in 30 to 50 feet — I had a 38-pounder come off there Tuesday morning on a live scup fished on a fish-finder rig with 60-pound fluoro leader, and that fish came right up out of the rocks on the last surge before the tide went flat. Once it slacks off, the bite dies fast out there — you've got maybe a ninety-minute window before the current quits and the fish drop back into the deeper holes and stop feeding. Southeast Light and the Chaunterelle have been quieter, more of an evening bite, umbrella rigs and tube-and-worm trolled slow along the drop-off in 60 to 90 feet.

Fluke have pulled a classic mid-summer move — out of the Great Salt Pond and the back-bay water, which has been running warm, and out into the inlet mouths and open ocean structure where that upwelled water is holding closer to 60 degrees. That colder, cleaner water is loaded with sand eels and squid right now, and the fluke know it. Best drift has been off the Coast Guard station on the outgoing, four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, bounced slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet. A few keepers to 5 pounds, more shorts than keepers if I'm honest, but the quality fish have been legitimately quality — thick, healthy, full of sand eels when we cleaned them.

The bonito news is real and it's spreading. With that cold wall gone, the corridor now runs from Block Island right up through Newport and into Point Judith, which is new for this early in July — usually we don't see that until the back half of the month. Small hardtails have been showing on the surface off Brenton Reef and around Beavertail on calm mornings, chasing bay anchovies in tight, fast-moving pods. If you see the birds working low and jumpy rather than diving hard, slow down — that's bonito, not bluefish, and they'll spook off a boat running full speed into the school. Small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dick spoons, cast ahead of the pod and worked fast on a straight retrieve, have been the ticket. It's not an all-day bite, more a dawn-and-dusk window, but the fact that it's happening at all this early tells me the water's ahead of schedule.

Bluefish have been scattered but present around Southwest Ledge and off the Charlestown breachway, mostly cocktail-sized fish on the troll, though a few boats have found bigger choppers mixed in with the bass on bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the last of the outgoing near the North Rip. Porgies remain the reliable bread-and-butter — sandworms and squid strips on double-hook rigs, anywhere there's structure in 20 to 40 feet, Great Salt Pond entrance and the rock piles off New Harbor both holding good numbers. Blackfish season's still closed here, so leave them be for now.

Looking ahead, the new-moon springs building toward the weekend are what I'd plan around. If the wind lays down Friday night like it's forecast to, I'd want to be on the Southwest Ledge for the sunset flood — that combination of maximum current and low light is when the true trophy fish show themselves. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is running the fluke drift off the Coast Guard station on the same tide, because that water isn't going anywhere either way. And keep an eye on the surface inshore — if this bonito push holds, Point Judith and Narragansett could be seeing steady action a full month ahead of the calendar.
